Calculation Details

How to convert watts to amps

Select DC, single-phase AC, or balanced three-phase AC. Enter real power in watts and voltage. AC calculations also use power factor because watts can be lower than apparent power when current and voltage are not perfectly in phase.

DC: A = W / V; single phase: A = W / (V x PF); three phase: A = W / (√3 x V line-to-line x PF)

Watts-to-amps example

A 1,200 W resistive load at 120 V and power factor 1.0 draws 10 A. At power factor 0.8, the same 1,200 W real load requires 12.5 A and 1,500 VA of apparent power.

Single-phase and three-phase voltage

For the three-phase formula, enter line-to-line RMS voltage and total three-phase real power. Do not enter per-phase power or line-to-neutral voltage into that formula. The US Department of Energy's industrial electrification framework gives the same √3 x power-factor relationship for a typical three-phase AC load.

Watts, VA, and VAR

Watts are real power doing useful work. Volt-amperes are apparent power carried by the source and conductors. Reactive volt-amperes represent the quadrature portion in this simplified sinusoidal model. DC uses power factor 1 and has no reactive-power result.

Continuous-load planning

Choose continuous-load planning to display 125% of calculated current. That is a planning reference, not a complete breaker or conductor selection. Use the electrical load calculator when continuous and noncontinuous loads must be entered separately.

Frequently asked questions

Is 1,500 watts always 12.5 amps?

Only at 120 V with power factor 1. Current changes with voltage, phase, and power factor.

Should I use equipment output watts?

Use electrical input power. Mechanical motor output and cooling capacity are not interchangeable with electrical input watts.

How do I reverse the conversion?

Use the amps to watts calculator with the same voltage, phase, and power factor.
